A. Memberships
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2( o) (3 )(iii)(B)(2) requires "[d ]ocumentation ofthe alien's membership
in associations in the field for which classification is sought, which require outstanding achievements of
their members, as judged by recognized national or international experts in their disciplines or fields."
USCIS determines ifthe association for which the person claims present or past membership requires that
members have outstanding achievements in the field as judged by recognized experts in the field. 2
The Petitioner provided evidence of the Beneficiary's membership with the United States Equestrian
Federation (USEF) and United States Eventing Association (USEA). As indicated by the Petitioner,
"[t]he USEF is the national governing body of equestrian sports," and "[t]he USEA, as the Recognized
Affiliate Association of the USEF for eventing, is the only organization that has approved national and
international rules for eventing." Moreover, the Petitioner states that "[t]he USEA is ... the national and
international regulator for the sport of eventing, enacting standards for training, competition and judging,
and ensuring these standards are met by the members," and "[t]he USEF promulgates the policies and
procedures for licensed officials."
The Petitioner further argues:
While membership in the USEA may seem simple at first glance, member competition up
the levels is strictly controlled by judges, officials and trainers subject to stringent national
and international standards. Both members, and horses, must qualify to compete at higher
1 See also generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, M.4(C)(2), https://www.uscis.gov/policymanual.
2 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
2
levels. For horses to qualify at each level and move up they must be trained at each level
by athletes such as the beneficiary.
The petition meets the criterion that the beneficiary is a member of associations in the
discipline of eventing which require outstanding achievements of their members, as
judged by recognized national or international experts in their discipline. The evidence
about the beneficiary's competitions establishes she is competing up to preliminary level
Associations may have multiple levels of membership.3 The petitioner must show that in order to obtain
the level of membership afforded to the beneficiary, the beneficiary was judged by recognized national
or international experts as having attained outstanding achievements in the field for which classification
is sought.4 According to the screenshots from useventing.com submitted by the Petitioner, "[t]here are
seven distinct levels of competition offered in USEA recognized competition starting with the lowest,
Beginner Novice, and ranging all the way up to the most difficult, Advanced." Specifically, the seven
levels, from easiest to hardest, consist of: Beginner Novice, Novice, Training, Modified, Preliminary,
Intermediate, and Advanced. The distinctions between Preliminary, Intermediate, and Advanced are as
follows:
• Preliminary - The Preliminary level is a moderate examination ofcompetitors and horses
in a regular training program preparing for two-star events.
• Intermediate - The Intermediate level is an examination ofincreasing technical difficulty,
preparing competitors and horses for three-star events.
• Advanced-The Advanced level is the highest national level ofhorse trials. It offers tests
ofsignificant difficulty designed to prepare competitors and horses for either four- or five­
star events.
Again, this regulatory criterion requires outstanding achievements as a condition for membership. Here,
the Petitioner did not demonstrate that the Beneficiary's competition at the Preliminary level is
tantamount to outstanding achievements. When compared to the Preliminary level, which is a "moderate
examination ofcompetitors and horse ... preparing for two-star events," ( emphasis added) the other two
higher levels requires significantly higher requirements. The Intermediate level requires "an examination
of increasing technical difficulty ... for three-star events" ( emphasis added), and the Advanced level "is
the highest national level of horse trials," "offers tests of sign[ficant difficulty," and "prepares ... either
four- or.five- star events" ( emphasis added). Although the Beneficiary performs at the fifth level, there
is a stark contrast to the two levels higher. The Petitioner did not establish that a moderate examination
in a regular training program to compete for two-star events rises to the level ofoutstanding achievements,
consistent with this regulatory criterion.
Moreover, the Petitioner did not show that membership is judged by recognized national or international
experts. In it's brief: the Petitioner specifically refers to "[p ]rocedures for recorded 'r' licensure, for
3 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
4 Id.
3
example, requires the completion of independent study, apprenticeship, sections of training on dressage,
cross country and jumping, and a final examination." While these reflect general "[r]equirements to
Obtain and Maintain 'r' Status," the Petitioner did not demonstrate that nationally or internationally
recognized experts judge the Preliminary level. 5
For the reasons discussed above, the Petitioner did not show the Beneficiary fulfills this criterion.

B. Published Materials
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(3) requires "[p]ublished material in professional or
major trade publications or major media about the alien, relating to the alien's work in the field for
which classification is sought, which shall include the title, date, and author ofsuch published material,
and any necessary translation." USCIS first determines whether the published material was related to
the person and the person's specific work in the field for which classification is sought. 6 USCIS then
determines whether the publication qualifies as a professional publication, major trade publication, or
major media publication. 7
The Petitioner contends:
[T]he evidence shows this criterion was established with the published results from the
unrecognized competition that the beneficiary completed with highly successful
results, resulting in an outstanding training for each of the horses under her training
care. See Exhibits 42-45. These results are correlated with photographs of the horse
and rider combinations and also awards in the form of ribbons. Therefore, contrary to
the conclusion in the decision, this criterion has been met.
The evidence the Petitioner refers consists of horse trial and event results from
~------------------------ along with photographs of ribbons
and purportedly of the Beneficiary competing in various events with handwritten comments.
However, the Petitioner did not demonstrate how the evidence reflects published material about the
Beneficiary and her work. Published material that includes only a brief citation or passing reference
to the beneficiary's work is not "about" the beneficiary, relating to the beneficiary's work in the field,
as required under this criterion. 8 Here, the evidence reflects trial and event results with the Beneficiary
mentioned among hundreds of competitors rather than published material about the Beneficiary. Cf,
Gadhave v. Thompson, No. 3:21-CV-2938-D, 2023 WL 6931334, at *3-4 (N.D. Tex. Oct. 19, 2023)
(upholding published material must be specifically about the applicant and focus on his personal work
in the relevant field, not merely relate to the applicant's work, mention his name, or include his photo);
Javakhadze v. Mayorkas, No. 3:21-CV-00617-E, 2023 WL 8037730, at *6 (N.D. Tex. Nov. 20, 2023)
(upholding USCIS' determination that the published materials discussed the outcomes of various
competitions, mentioning the plaintiff in passing as it related to competition results, rather than
published material about him).
5 See screenshots "US Equestrian Licensed Officials Policies and Procedures" submitted by the Petitioner.
6 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
7 Id.
8 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
4
Moreover, the Petitioner does not argue, nor does the record contain evidence that any of the websites
reflect professional or major trade publications or major media status. In evaluating whether a
submitted publication is a professional publication, major trade publication, or major media, relevant
factors include the intended audience (for professional and major trade publications) and the relative
circulation, readership, or viewership (for major trade publications and other major media). 9 The
Petitioner did not establish that the Beneficiary received published material about her and her work in
professional or major trade publication or major media. 10
Accordingly, the Petitioner did not demonstrate the Beneficiary satisfies this criterion.

Petitioner claims the Beneficiary's eligibility for two additional categories (awards under 8 C.F.R.
§ 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(]) and capacity under 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(7)), we need not reach these
grounds because the Beneficiary cannot fulfill the initial evidentiary requirement ofat least three under
